A $450 million accelerated charitable contribution impacted quarterly EPS by approximately $1, though underlying ROE remained strong at approximately 20% excluding this item.

Impact of emerging technologies like tokenization on market making

BREAKING NEWS

China rattled the memory trade on Tuesday. But by the close, investors had made up their minds about who actually has a problem. It's the DRAM makers.

ChangXin Memory Technologies, China's biggest memory chipmaker, said over the weekend it had made real progress on a new chip design that crams more data into less space, CNBC reports. Asia took it badly: SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in Seoul and Samsung fell over 7%.

U.S. memory stocks opened in the same hole, with nearly every name down 5% to 8%. Then the buyers showed up.

Seagate, Western Digital and SanDisk clawed back almost all of it and closed down less than 2%. Micron didn't get the same rescue. It finished down 3.6%, its second straight loss. SK Hynix's U.S. shares fell 3.2%. The S&P 500 ended flat.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

The split makes sense. CXMT makes DRAM, the same chips Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung sell. A Chinese rival closing the gap is a direct shot at their pricing. Hard drives and flash storage are a different business.

Some analysts think the market overreacted. Rayliant's Phillip Wool told CNBC that CXMT still hasn't shown it can produce at scale, and it isn't a threat yet in the high-bandwidth memory chips that power AI. He said the selloff showed "how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment."

Still, the CXMT news looks more like an excuse than a cause. Memory stocks were already well off their highs before the weekend, with Micron down about a quarter from its peak and Western Digital down by half. Investors have been hunting for a reason to take profits on the AI trade's biggest winners. China handed them one, and they used it on the stocks with the most to lose.

COMMENTARY

Our analysts just identified a stock with the potential to be the next Nvidia. Tell us how you invest and we'll show you why it's our #1 pick. Tap here.

Aurora Cannabis may have a second suitor, and its fate could rest with BAT, the tobacco giant behind Camel and Newport.

BAT-backed Organigram, a Canadian cannabis producer, has explored talks for a potential deal with Aurora, Moby reported Friday. The deal, whether a merger or some other tie-up, would set up a fight with Curaleaf, which upsized its hostile bid for Aurora last week from $4 to $5 per share. Most of that bid is Curaleaf stock.

The prize is Europe. Aurora operates EU-GMP certified facilities, the pharmaceutical-grade standard required to export medical cannabis into Germany and most of the EU. Few Canadian producers hold the certification, and it takes years to earn. Germany's medical market has boomed since the country loosened its rules in 2024.

That fits Organigram's international export ambitions. It recently bought Sanity Group, a German cannabis distributor, and is now eyeing Aurora's EU-GMP facility, like Curaleaf.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

But Organigram can't do this alone. Analyst Pablo Zuanic, who's been covering cannabis stocks a long time, did the math: He models an Organigram bid of C$8.55, or $6 per share, which matches the cap Curaleaf set on its own offer.

Organigram has more sales than Aurora, but it's worth less than half as much by market cap: $193 million to $416 million. Organigram would likely have to issue so many new shares that Aurora holders would end up owning 51% of the combined company.

That makes it BAT's call. The tobacco giant already owns nearly 30% of Organigram, and Zuanic reasons a C$60 million cash injection would put a real bid on the table.

Curaleaf isn't tapped out either. Zuanic thinks it could raise the cash portion of its offer from $1 to $2.50 a share before debt becomes a problem. Of course, nothing may yet materialize from these discussions. But the real question is: does BAT want Aurora?

The best dividend stocks are often the ones that raise their payouts at high rates. While their yields may not be high today, businesses that are willing and able to grow their payouts significantly could reward long-term investors with much higher dividend payments in the future.

Three stocks that have doubled their payouts in just the past five years include Eli Lilly (NYSE:LLY), Tractor Supply Company (NASDAQ:TSCO), and American Express (NYSE:AXP). Here's a look at why these dividend stocks can make for excellent pillars to build a portfolio around.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Eli Lilly

Eli Lilly may just be one of the most underrated dividend stocks to own. Investors may overlook it because its yield is fairly low at just 0.6%, which is far below the S&P 500 average of around 1.1%.

But in recent years, Eli Lilly has been one of the hottest growth stocks to own in the healthcare sector. It's the only healthcare company in the trillion-dollar club. The tremendous growth its GLP-1 drugs have generated for the business has made it a go-to option for growth investors seeking a safe investment to hang on to. And with the stock trading at 24 times its estimated future profits (which are based on analyst expectations), it's not a terribly expensive-looking stock when factoring in its growth opportunities.

The company's current quarterly dividend of $1.73 is just over twice what it was paying its shareholders back in 2021, when the dividend was $0.85. Due to the company's tremendous growth over the years, there's still room for even more increases, as its payout ratio is modest at just 22%.

Tractor Supply Company

Investors can collect a higher payout from Tractor Supply Company, as its yield is up to 2.9% right now. The retail stock has been struggling this year, declining 33% thus far in 2026, as challenging economic conditions are weighing on its business. The company, which sells a wide range of products for rural customers, however, remains relatively resilient, posting $1 billion in profit over the past four quarters, on revenue of around $15.8 billion.

The stock currently pays investors $0.24 per quarter. It underwent a 5-for-1 stock split in 2024, which means the $0.52 it was paying in 2021 would be $0.104 on a split-adjusted basis. Tractor Supply's dividend, therefore, has increased by 131% since then. The company's payout ratio is around 50%, which is still very manageable and leaves room for it to increase the dividend in future years, even without strong growth.

SpaceX Wants $40 Billion in New Debt, and It'll Need Hundreds of Billions More to Achieve Musk's Vision

Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX) raised $86 billion with its IPO. It then tapped the debt market for another $25 billion. Now, it's looking to get another $40 billion in financing to pursue its massive artificial intelligence (AI) build-out.

Elon Musk's company reportedly reached out to Apollo Global Management and several banks to help it purchase $40 billion worth of Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) GPUs. But Musk could be just getting started. SpaceX still needs a colossal amount of capital to achieve the CEO's vision.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Here's what that means for investors.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
SpaceX needs a ton of capital to build its business

SpaceX generated $12.5 billion of revenue in the first six months of 2026 while capital expenditures climbed to $28.5 billion. The vast majority of that capex is tied to its AI infrastructure build-out.

SpaceX has made a huge bet on artificial intelligence as the future of the business. It acquired Musk's xAI at the start of the year and plans to develop orbital data centers. In the meantime, it's building plain-old terrestrial data centers full of Nvidia GPUs.

Management said it ended the second quarter with 1.4 gigawatts of compute capacity. Musk said he expects SpaceX to end the year with over 2 gigawatts of compute during the company's second-quarter earnings call. For 2027, Musk said its capacity could "be closer to 10 gigawatts of compute than 5 gigawatts of compute."

To put that in perspective, Amazon had just over 10 gigawatts of compute deployed as of June, according to Jefferies data. Microsoft and Alphabet had just over 5 gigawatts. That said, all three expect to have huge amounts coming online over the next couple of years.

Nvidia estimates the cost of deploying its chips is about $60 billion per gigawatt. To go from 2 gigawatts to 10 gigawatts in 2027 will cost SpaceX around $480 billion in capital expenditures. And that's just for data center builds. SpaceX is also working to get its Starship fully reusable rocket ready to launch multiple times per week. It's also continuing to deploy Starlink satellites and buying radio spectrum licenses to expand its internet service with a direct-to-mobile service.

Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas wrote in his initial note on SpaceX that it would require an average of $84 billion in external capital per year through 2034 before it started producing positive cash flow. That's $672 billion total. Musk is apparently planning to front-load those capital needs, and that creates a huge risk for investors.

title: Why Applied Materials Sank Today

Why Applied Materials Sank Today

Shares of semiconductor equipment supplier Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) sank on Tuesday, down 7.2% as of 3:53 p.m. EDT.

Applied Materials unveiled its $5 billion EPIC research center in Silicon Valley yesterday, a new facility meant to aid co-innovation with Applied's customers.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Today, Applied followed up on yesterday's event with an investor presentation. While the company painted a bullish picture of the future, the presentation omitted a key data point many investors would have liked to know. Given recent jitters over the sustainability of the AI build-out, it's no wonder the limited disclosure triggered a sell-off.

Applied projects some things to 2030, but not overall revenue

At today's investor breakfast, Applied touted its leadership across etch, deposition, e-beam metrology, and advanced packaging tools that will be critical to modern AI systems. In particular, Applied highlighted its leadership in tools for the DRAM, leading-edge logic, and advanced packaging sectors as underpinning growth, as these semiconductor sub-segments are set to benefit most from the growth of agentic AI.

Additionally, management advertised that artificial intelligence is making its operations more efficient, which should boost profitability.

Aside from the technology updates and presentations, CFO Brice Hill also gave guidance on a few financial metrics. Thanks to strong growth in the chip equipment sector, Applied expects its adjusted (non-GAAP) gross margin to expand to roughly 54% by 2030, with an operating margin of approximately 40%. In 2025, adjusted gross margin was 48.8%, while adjusted operating margin was 30.2%. So, the 2030 guidance would mark a strong five percentage point and 10 percentage point improvement, respectively, which is significant.

However, Applied didn't articulate how large its revenue will grow by that time. Instead, management disclosed only its anticipated market share gain and the growth in its services segment. Service revenue encompasses tool maintenance and a data service that helps customers improve yields.

By 2030, Applied expects to gain two percentage points of wafer front-end equipment (WFE) market share. Meanwhile, it also projects services revenue to grow to "over" $12 billion. Last year in fiscal 2025, Applied Global Services amounted to roughly $6.4 billion.
